This research proposes a novel, hierarchical, on-demand data collection method for Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) that utilizes a combination of cluster heads and virtual boundaries to minimize energy usage and optimize link transmission. The proposed method involves designating cluster heads to manage local data and relay it to a sink node, while also creating virtual boundaries to partition the network into smaller sections. By using a bidirectional link quality estimation technique, the method can accurately assess the transmission quality between nodes and improve overall link efficiency. The method is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate significant energy savings and improved link quality compared to existing protocols.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the application of deep contextualized objects detection methods, including an analysis of contextual object detection scenarios, the data used to train these models, the approaches used to train them, and the models developed. Contextual object detection models leverage the relationships between objects within an image to enhance the accuracy of image annotation. A key finding is that simple models capturing object-object relationships can outperform complex deep learning architectures in certain object detection tasks.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate a system of elliptic equations of Kirchhoff type, which incorporates large growth nonlinearities and exceptional Trudinger-Moser type growth terms. We establish the compactness of the embedding, apply the Nehari manifold technique, and utilize topological arguments to obtain at least one nontrivial weak solution for the given system.

We establish new bounds for the probability mass of the sum of independently multiplied Bernoulli random variables conditioned on an event, where the variables exhibit limited independence and pairwise negative correlation. These bounds exhibit improved performance compared to existing inequalities like Bernstein's and Chebyshev's in certain scenarios. Notably, our bounds for negatively correlated variables do not depend on the total number of variables, offering an advantage over the standard method of applying the XOR-lemma to achieve $k$-independence. This alternative approach would have resulted in bounds with an undesirable factor of $\log_2 n$.

Let O be a complete local Noetherian ring that contains a field with characteristic p > 0 as well as a primitive (p-1)th root of unity, with the property of being Henselian with respect to its maximal ideal. The main focus of this research is to establish an equivalence of categories between finite locally free modules with integrally admissible linearized differential operators over the power series ring in one variable in positive characteristic, and locally free modules with integral étale representations over the corresponding étale site, with the added condition of being tamely ramified at the power of p. The established equivalence provides a torsor-theoretic description of the prfπ stacks associated with linearized differential modules over power series rings.

This study investigates the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in SIDIS, specifically focusing on the correlation between the azimuthal angles of two created hadrons. To analyze this effect, we calculated the cosine asymmetry in SIDIS using the color glass condensate model, taking into account the longitudinal spin dependence of the quark distribution and the dihadron color glass condensate effect. Our calculations demonstrate that the cosine asymmetry in SIDIS can be a significant indicator of the dihadron $c$-shaped structure. Moreover, our results suggest that the cosine asymmetry in SIDIS can be utilized to experimentally investigate the cos$\phi_R$ component of the TMD distribution, providing a means to directly probe the structure of the color glass condensate.

We've derived a new, linear transformation that converts a set of linearly independent solutions for a massless scalar field's wave equation in four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space to a corresponding set of solutions for the same type of field's equation in four-dimensional de Sitter space. This relationship holds true for any non-zero values of the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetime curvatures, denoted as $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_1^{-1}$, respectively. The transformation can be viewed as an extension of de Sitter space, and the corresponding field in de Sitter space is massless. The relationship between the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spaces can be further understood through the lens of Fock's transformation, which has been applied to a scalar field's equations of motion in four-dimensional Minkowski space.

Let $(V, \omega)$ and $(V, \sigma)$ be two non-degenerate symplectic forms defined on a vector space $V$. A transformation $T$ that maintains these forms is referred to as a symplectic conversion from $(V, \omega)$ to $(V, \sigma)$. When the two forms are equivalent, the existence of such a transformation is guaranteed. However, when the forms are not equivalent, the existence of such a transformation is not. In this paper, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a transformation based on the canonical forms of $\omega$ and $\sigma$. Additionally, we explore the relationship between symplectic conversions and the conversion of quadratic forms.

This study proposes a novel entity recommendation approach that leverages Wikipedia and incorporates an entity's hierarchical structure to enhance its performance. We utilize Wikipedia's layered graph representation to capture an entity's intrinsic properties and interconnections. A combination of matrix factorization and deep learning techniques is employed to develop a hybrid model that outperforms conventional matrix factorization methods. We also explore the impact of different knowledge graph construction strategies and entity extraction methods on the model's effectiveness. Our approach is evaluated through a comprehensive set of experiments on Wikipedia's top 1000 ranked pages, demonstrating its superiority over alternative knowledge graph-based entity recommendation methods.

The practice of exchanging kidney transplants has been in place for some time now, yet its full potential is not being realized. Many individuals on the kidney transplant waiting list are being denied the opportunity due to incompatible blood types, as they are unable to find a suitable donor. This issue is particularly prevalent among African Americans, who are disproportionately affected. We investigate a novel approach to kidney transplantation that involves exchanging incompatible kidneys among three-party groups, and demonstrate through a mathematical model that this approach can significantly increase the number of transplants performed, providing substantial benefits to those currently unable to receive a transplant.

The concepts of implicit ties and relationships between variables have long been explored in the fields of statistics and machine learning. This area of study has seen a significant rise in interest, particularly in applications to machine reading comprehension and natural language inference. The primary objective of this research is to provide an in-depth examination of implicit ties and their underlying principles. The study also aims to highlight the current challenges and potential applications of implicit ties in machine reading comprehension and natural language inference, as well as in other domains. The research is conducted from a probabilistic perspective, which is essential for a comprehensive understanding of implicit ties. The study is among the first to offer a unified overview of implicit ties from this perspective.

NLP techniques have gained significant attention in recent years due to their
ability to analyze financial documents, which contain vast amounts of unstructured
textual information. As these documents often reflect the sentiments of market
participants, sentiment analysis has become a crucial step in transforming this
data into a usable format. In this study, we investigate whether state-of-the-art
word representations, such as GloVe, truly grasp the semantic meanings of financial
terms, particularly those that convey emotional sentiments. To test this, we
developed a sentiment classification model using the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment
Dictionary and compared its performance against embeddings-based classifiers. Our
results indicate that classifiers using pre-trained embeddings outperformed our
baseline, but the improvement was marginal. Furthermore, our analysis of the
GloVe representations of financial terms with distinct polarities suggests that
these terms are not distinctly represented in the embedded space.
This paper presents the MISO-OFDM and SISO-OFDM equivalents to the previously discussed concepts.

This research introduces a novel hybrid method that combines level-set and embedded boundary techniques to tackle complex interface dynamics, including the process of solidification and melting. The level-set method is employed to model the boundary between solid and liquid phases, while the embedded boundary technique discretizes the domain into small elements, enabling a detailed representation of material properties. The level-set method's ability to handle topological changes is complemented by the embedded boundary technique's high-order accuracy, resulting in a method that is both precise and capable of modeling intricate phenomena. The proposed technique is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments that simulate the process of solidification and melting, yielding results that are in close agreement with theoretical predictions. The results indicate that the method is an effective tool for modeling a wide range of applications, from industrial processes to natural phenomena.

In the 1970s, J. A. Kripke highlighted the rarity of unary connectives in language, a feature more prevalent in artificial languages than in natural ones. This paper builds on Kripke's work by exploring the concept of unarity in both artificial and natural languages, particularly in relation to tense and modality. It challenges the traditional interpretation of these modalities as future-oriented and instead proposes a view of them as representing possible "spins" in language. This perspective is then expanded to incorporate the principles of quantum language, a framework that combines the concepts of language and quantum mechanics.

In multiplayer games, finding the best strategy to achieve equilibrium is a complex challenge. A new method has been developed to suggest equilibrium strategies for games that humans can understand and act on. This approach uses a neural network to model the game and learns the equilibrium strategies through reinforcement learning. It then uses a technique called value decomposition to break down the rewards into individual player components, allowing it to suggest explanations for the strategies in terms of individual player goals. This method was tested on several games, including a simple two-player game and a more complex multi-player game, and showed that the suggested explanations were accurate and helpful. This method can be used to design better AI agents that can act in equilibrium and receive feedback on the effectiveness of their strategies.

A novel dynamic graph model has been developed in response to a well-known issue in network science - the "arms race" paradox. This new model builds on the foundational concept of preferential attachment but incorporates an additional mechanism: the deliberate rewiring of nodes to avoid highly connected nodes. By mimicking a preventive strategy to evade the spread of infection, this modified network model was analyzed in the context of an epidemic spreading through a variant of the configuration model. The study reveals that the deliberate avoidance rewiring can significantly impact the epidemic's spread, effectively halting the infection's transmission when the avoided rewiring rate surpasses the preferential attachment rate. In contrast, a net increase in edges due to both mechanisms leads to unbounded component sizes and inevitable infection of all nodes. Furthermore, the study highlights the emergence of a novel, self-similar structure within the largest component when the deliberate avoidance rewiring rate exceeds the preferential attachment rate.

This research focuses on the geometric properties of a specific type of manifold, the nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, and examines how Cotton vectors and solitons interact within the context of these manifolds. More specifically, we investigate the conditions under which a pair of linearly independent vector fields can form a Cotton soliton on a nearly Kenmotsu 3-$h$-manifold, and it is proven that such a condition cannot be satisfied.

This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the framework used in fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data. It delves into the statistical methods employed in fitting, including the discussion of key parameters such as $\chi^2$, covariance matrices, and data weighting. Various approaches to determining PDF uncertainties are examined, covering both linear and non-linear methods, as well as the impact of theoretical systematics. To facilitate future research, a set of recommendations for the PDF fitting community is proposed.

To improve the efficiency of training neural networks, the method of vectorized mini-batch processing is commonly employed, but this approach may inadvertently introduce bias into the data, potentially hindering the performance of the resulting policy. In order to overcome this limitation, a novel technique called variance diminution based experience replay (VDER) has been proposed, which selectively retains data that minimizes the overall variance of the processed mini-batches. VDER has been successfully applied to both value function approximation and policy optimization problems, and experimental results have demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed and final solution quality when compared to traditional vectorized training methods.

We present PyCommute, a Python library that facilitates the efficient use of commuting operators for tasks such as Hamiltonian construction and solving of the time-independent Schrödinger equation. By leveraging symbolic computation, PyCommute paves the way for LibCommute, an optimized C++ library that forms its performance-optimized core. Both libraries are designed to be interoperable, allowing users to easily integrate LibCommute into their existing Python-based workflows with PyCommute.

We have conducted comprehensive angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy on the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ superconductor, revealing the following electronic structure characteristics: a single electron-like hole pocket at the $\Gamma$ point, an elliptical hole pocket at the M point, and an elliptical electron pocket at the X point. Our findings also indicate that the superconducting gap at the $\Gamma$ point has an isotropic s-wave symmetry, while the gap at the M point exhibits an anisotropic s-wave symmetry with a maximum value of 2.5 meV. In contrast, the gap at the X point has a maximum value of 1.5 meV and is also anisotropic s-wave-like symmetry.

Two approaches to the supersymmetric partition function have been examined, specifically the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization technique. A connection between these methods has been established, revealing that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is equivalent to integrating the superbosonization differential equation. This finding has been verified through explicit calculations of the supermatrices, including Gaussian and chiral ensembles.

The measurement of the top quark polarization in a specific type of top quark production, not involving Higgs bosons, provides valuable insights into the fundamental properties of the top quark. This study presents a measurement of the top quark polarization by analyzing the angular distribution of the leptons originating from the top quark decay. Utilizing data collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 49.6 fb^-1 from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the measurement focuses on events containing one electron or muon with significant missing transverse momentum. The analysis restricts the sample to events where the lepton originates from the semi-leptonic decay of the top quark. The resulting measurement of the top quark polarization is found to be in agreement with the Standard Model predictions, with an asymmetry value of 0.011 +/- 0.011 (statistical uncertainty) +/- 0.006 (systematic uncertainty).

We utilized $\beta$-detected NMR to examine the spin dynamics and metallic properties of LaNiO3/ LaAlO3 superlattices with varying LaNiO3 thickness. Our study revealed that the metallic phase of LaNiO3 exhibits slow, non-thermal $^8$Li spin dynamics and a gap in the NMR spectrum, which are indicative of short-range magnetic order. These features are more pronounced in thinner LaNiO3 films and diminish as the film's thickness increases. Our findings suggest that the magnetic order in the LaNiO3 metal is described by a dynamic order parameter, which is consistent with recent theoretical predictions.

In our analysis of current conversational systems, we've identified three key areas for improvement: the limited range of programmatic actions available to the system, the lack of complexity in the system actions, and the limited diversity of conversation topics. To address these issues, we've developed a highly branching dialogue testbed that challenges the current capabilities of conversational agents. We've created a set of branching conversation topics categorized into four types: task-oriented, multi-step tasks, multi-discourse topics, and social interactions. We've also designed a set of programs that can be executed by the system, allowing for more sophisticated interactions. We've evaluated the testbed using both existing methods and human testers, and the results indicate that the testbed is suitable for developing and evaluating conversational systems that engage in complex, diverse conversations.

This research examines how to optimize data transfer in a wireless system that uses an intelligently reconfigurable surface, taking into account real-world factors like correlated signal fading and limited antenna capacity. We develop a mathematical model to estimate the long-term average data transfer rates under these conditions and reconfigure surface designs to maximize these rates, considering two different methods for setting the device's phase shifts.

We have developed a set of initial conditions for modified gravity simulations that are based on a general framework. This framework allows us to create nested particle distributions in three stages, with the outer stage being controlled by a parameter that represents the type of gravitational theory being used. This framework is applicable to $\Lambda$CDM, $f(R)$ gravity, and D6 models. We have created an initial conditions generator that can create these multi-particle distributions in an efficient manner. This generator is capable of creating simulations with up to $10^7$ particles in three dimensions. We have also conducted simulations using this generator for different gravitational theories, with the simulations being run for different cosmological times. These simulations have been compared to their $\Lambda$CDM counterparts, with the results being consistent with each other. We have also analyzed the effects of a non-zero value of the parameter $\phi$ on the simulation results, with the effects being minimal. We have also investigated the relationship between the number of particles used in the inner and outer stages of the simulation, with the results being consistent with each other. We have also found that the choice of the gravitational theory being used has a minimal effect on the simulation results. These findings have important implications for the interpretation of future cosmological surveys.

Miller and Sheffield established a connection between the Gaussian free field and a collection of Schramm-Loewevian evolutions driven by a two-dimensional Coulomb gas, yet the interaction between these evolutions and their boundaries remains unclear. In this study, we extend this relationship to include cases where the Loewevian evolutions may intersect or interact with the Gaussian free field. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Loewevian evolutions can be linked to a one-dimensional Dyson Brownian motion, while also determining the precise boundary conditions and interaction between the particles and the Gaussian free field. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for the values at which these evolutions may become trapped.

MediaWiki, commonly known as Wikipedia's underlying technology, offers a robust and flexible platform for both web and non-web use. Its open-source nature and extensive suite of available tools make it suitable for a wide range of applications. To take full advantage of MediaWiki, developers often utilize specialized tools and libraries, commonly referred to as "mwores." However, these tools can be challenging to use due to the need for familiarity with both Python and the MediaWiki API. To address this, we present an open-source package called "WorkingWiki" that streamlines the use of MediaWiki-derived tools for collaborative research projects. This package is user-friendly and can be easily customized to meet specific project requirements. We demonstrate its capabilities through its release on the open source platform PyPI.

To understand how turbulent jet flames react to acoustic forcing, a linearized model is used to analyze the interaction between the flame and its surroundings. This analysis focuses on the relationship between the heat released by the flame and the fluctuations in the surrounding air pressure. A linearized, one-dimensional model is proposed to predict this relationship using an "active flame" concept. This active flame concept is based on the assumption that the flame's behavior can be described by a linearized version of the Bernoulli equation. The model is validated using experimental data from a turbulent jet flame that is burning methane in air. The model accurately predicts the phase and magnitude of the flame's response to acoustic forcing, and is shown to be robust across a range of acoustic frequencies. The model is also used to analyze the reaction of the flame to acoustic waves of different wavelengths. The results show that the flame's reaction is most pronounced when the acoustic waves have a short wavelength, and that the reaction is less pronounced when the waves have a long wavelength. A novel approach has been developed to identify and classify topological properties in dynamic systems through the application of homotopy theory. This method was specifically tailored to investigate the behavior of stars, focusing on oscillatory patterns in their outer layers. By representing the oscillatory modes of a star as a vector in a topological space, researchers discovered a conservation law that allows for the classification of these modes into distinct topological groups. This classification reveals the presence of a "twist" in the oscillatory patterns, which corresponds to a specific property of the star's surface known as helicity. This helicity is directly related to a measurable quantity called the rotational frequency of the star. The study found that this relationship holds true for a wide range of stars, including those with varying densities and rotational speeds. The implications of this discovery are far-reaching, as it suggests that the behavior of stars can be understood through the lens of topological principles, which may have applications to the study of other celestial bodies and the universe as a whole.

A novel technique has been developed to detect two types of collective behavior in dynamical networks: the presence of traveling chimera states and synchronized clusters. This method is highly effective, even when dealing with complex systems exhibiting multiple coexisting states or chaotic dynamics. The underlying principle of the technique involves a specific metric that quantifies the degree of synchronization among network nodes. When this metric is plotted over time, it reveals distinct patterns that indicate the presence of these collective states. The method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through its ability to accurately identify traveling chimera states in a network of coupled oscillators, a network of neurons, and a dynamical system with multiple layers. The universal nature of the detection scheme suggests its potential for broader applications in understanding the behavior of various types of networks.

Our study investigates two-dimensional lattice gases in a two-dimensional square lattice, focusing on how clusters form and evolve. We use a Monte Carlo simulation to examine the impact of site-to-site interaction on cluster behavior. The simulation involves particles that adhere to neighboring sites based on attractive interactions and can jump to adjacent sites within the lattice. The study reveals that an increase in the number of particles that stick to each other leads to the formation of larger clusters. The cluster size distribution follows a power law, indicating the presence of scale-free behavior. The phase transition from a disordered to an ordered state is characterized by the emergence of a giant cluster that spans the entire lattice. The order parameter, which measures the fraction of the giant cluster, exhibits hysteresis, indicating that the system's behavior depends on its history. The study also reveals that the system's response to an external field is influenced by the strength of the interaction between particles. The results are compared to previous studies on the same system, and the implications of the findings are discussed.

Conflicting updates pose a significant challenge to the performance of modern data storage systems. To mitigate this issue, designers are increasingly turning to conflict-free replicated data structures, which sacrifice update latency in favor of eliminating the need to resolve conflicts. However, a lack of unified guidelines has hindered the development of these data structures, resulting in designs that are often ad-hoc and lack consistency. We aim to address this gap by providing a comprehensive design framework for conflict-free structures, which includes a set of abstract operations, conflict management strategies, and design principles. Our framework is illustrated through a case study on the conflict-free set data structure, which includes an evaluation of design choices and performance outcomes.

This research provides a comprehensive analysis of 18 diverse human traits, ranging from height to educational attainment. By integrating functional genomic data with genome-wide association studies, we explored the distribution of association signals across different functional elements and chromatin states. Our findings reveal that the locations of associations vary significantly by trait, and that certain elements, such as active enhancers, are disproportionately enriched in associations for highly heritable traits. We also examined the relationship between associations and trait genetic architecture, and found that the number of independent signals and loci explaining a substantial proportion of heritability are disproportionately found in highly accessible genomic regions. Our results have important implications for understanding the connections between gene regulation and complex human traits.

This study delves into the complexities of identifying and analyzing rare events in minor systems during experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The challenges posed by high background noise and limited detection capabilities are examined, along with strategies to overcome these obstacles. The paper specifically investigates the production of heavy exotic particles in such rare scenarios, highlighting the significance of this research in the context of searching for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

A significant proportion of the neutron star X-ray binary population that exhibits short recurrence intervals of less than one year is concentrated in the inner 4.5 kiloparsecs of the Milky Way. This region is characterized by a high mass-shining area ratio, which is believed to be the primary factor influencing the recurrence interval distribution. A simple model based on this influence is presented, and its predictions are compared to the actual observed data. This simple model accurately replicates the key features of the recurrence interval distribution within this region, and is further applied to estimate the number of X-ray binaries that are in a quiescent state near the center of the Milky Way. These estimates are in line with the number of X-ray binaries that have been observed using the Chandra X-ray Observatory. A simple model is also proposed to describe the recurrence interval distribution of the black hole X-ray binaries in the Milky Way. This simple model is also used to estimate the number of quiescent X-ray binaries that contain a black hole, and these estimates are in line with the number of X-ray binaries that have been observed using the Chandra X-ray Observatory in a 10-kiloparsec radius around the center of the Milky Way. This is in line with the number of quiescent X-ray binaries that contain a black hole that are expected to be present in the inner 4.5 kiloparsecs of the Milky Way.

The dynamics of a solitary wide binary system can be significantly impacted by a solitary third body, making it challenging to draw conclusions about the gravitational force at large distances. To circumvent this issue, researchers are instead focusing on the collective behavior of wide binary systems within our galaxy. By utilizing Gaia data, we have identified 1150 such systems with distances greater than 1000 astronomical units, and found that 90% of these systems adhere to the Keplerian model. However, when we account for the influence of the Galactic tidal field and passing stars using a Jacobi ellipsoid model, the fit becomes even better. Consequently, the data does not provide conclusive evidence for deviations from expected behavior in wide binary systems.

Radio sources that are compact and faint, known as SCFRS, are extensively used in cosmological studies and investigations into active galactic nuclei. However, their properties are not fully understood due to observational limitations. This study employs a stacking analysis to examine the physical and physical kinematic characteristics of SCFRS, exploring how these features are influenced by angular size. By analyzing radio spectra, spectral energy distributions, and molecular gas mass ratios, we found that the spectra of SCFRS are generally top-heavy, with a mean spectral index of -0.79. This study also found that SCFRS are often super-Eddington sources, with an estimated Eddington ratio of 0.41. The Eddington ratio increases with angular size, with a value of 0.51 for sources larger than 1 arcsecond. Furthermore, the molecular gas mass ratio of SCFRS is estimated at 0.21, with a higher ratio of 0.31 for sources with a larger angular size.

The study reveals that the interaction between the star's pulsations and magnetic field lines can lead to the creation of multiple, coexisting shock waves that can significantly impact the behavior of the system. This paper provides a proof of a previously unverified result, which states that there is a one-to-one correspondence between a specific set of non-mathematical, algebraic structures of dimension twelve over a field and a set of algebraic systems over the same field. Additionally, this proof supplies the necessary details to fill in a gap in an uncompleted proof from a prior study.

This research proposes new ways to control the flow of heat and electrical energy in solid materials by exploiting their vibrational properties. Specifically, it demonstrates that certain materials can experience enhanced interactions between electrons and their surrounding lattice when they move as a whole. By applying this concept to specific crystal structures, scientists found that moving the entire material can significantly change the flow of heat, potentially leading to new methods for controlling thermal conductivity. This effect is particularly pronounced in certain materials with high mobility, where the difference in electron-phonon and acoustic-phonon scattering rates can be used to create unique ways to manipulate heat flow.

$\tau$-tilting theory was first introduced nearly a decade ago by Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten, and it has since become a key area of study in representation theory. This field of science has been relatively underexplored until now, and this lecture aims to provide a basic overview of $\tau$-tilting theory, with an emphasis on clarity. The lecture will introduce the necessary background and key concepts, and will also showcase some of the most significant recent research in this field.

The success of neural dialogue systems relies on their ability to generate diverse and engaging responses. While previous approaches have focused on improving coherence, they often overlook the need for variety in natural language understanding. To address this gap, we propose incorporating Natural Language Inference (NLI) into neural sequence-to-sequence models to better capture the semantic diversity in multi-turn conversations. Our proposed method, called NeVar, leverages Neumann's sampling to generate diverse responses while maintaining coherence through the incorporation of attention mechanisms. Experimental results on the multi-turn conversational dataset show that NeVar outperforms existing diversity baselines in terms of both diversity and coherence metrics.

Automated driving systems are being developed with safety as a primary concern, and the hazardous action detection module is crucial to preventing accidents. The detection of hazardous actions, such as pedestrians or vehicles that may cause accidents, is being improved through the use of deep learning and computer vision techniques. A deep learning-based approach is proposed to classify pedestrians in short video clips from a car's onboard camera as either hazardous or non-hazardous. The proposed approach involves a two-stage process, where the first stage uses a segmentation mask transfer method to accurately identify pedestrians in video clips, and the second stage uses a deep spatiotemporal network to classify the action. The approach is tested on 1000 video clips from the NuScenes dataset, and the results show that it can accurately detect hazardous actions with a mean average precision of 0.700. The proposed approach is also compared to a baseline approach, and the results show that it outperforms the baseline approach in terms of accuracy.

Researchers have observed young, rotating brown dwarfs that are still in the process of contracting, and they have found that these objects have not yet reached their minimum radius due to the centrifugal force caused by their rapid rotation. To better understand this phenomenon, a new hydrodynamical simulation framework has been developed to model rotating low-mass objects, specifically those with masses similar to that of the Sun and high angular velocities that are close to their mass-shedding limits. The simulation results show that the object's radius decreases as its angular velocity increases, and that the object's shape changes from spherical to oblate due to the centrifugal force. The simulation also reveals that the object's internal structure is affected by its rotation, and that the object's thermal evolution is slowed down due to the mixing of hot and cool gases caused by the Coriolis force. The simulation results are in good agreement with the observations of young, rotating brown dwarfs, and they provide a valuable tool for understanding the internal structure and thermal evolution of these objects.

Hadronic final-state interactions are responsible for the complex patterns of decay amplitudes observed in experiments, which cannot be fully understood without a thorough investigation. This is particularly evident in the data collected from experiments, where the production mechanisms and detector responses introduce additional effects that distort the observed patterns. To address this challenge, a new framework has been developed that allows for the simultaneous fitting of production effects, detector responses, and decay amplitudes, enabling a more accurate and efficient analysis of amplitude data. This approach is demonstrated through the analysis of $K^+K^-\pi^+\pi^-$ decays of $B^0_d$ mesons, where the effective $K\pi$ scattering amplitudes are used to model the decay amplitudes. The results show that this approach allows for a significant reduction in the number of parameters required to fit the data, while maintaining a high level of accuracy. Furthermore, this approach is shown to be applicable to a wide range of decays, making it a valuable tool for amplitude analysis in particle physics experiments.

Observations of some high-energy bursts (BHRs) and their optical afterglows show a pattern where larger energies correlate with longer times and higher expansion rates. To understand this, we propose that the burst energy and its surrounding medium's density are directly related, which would explain this observed progression. By using this relationship, we can derive a new formula that aligns with our observations and allows us to estimate the density of the surrounding medium based on the burst's energy and afterglow brightness. This new formula is then used to analyze the observed BHRs and their afterglows, revealing a consistent pattern across different energies and times when assuming a direct relationship between the burst energy and the surrounding medium's density. However, the estimated BHRs' energies are significantly lower than the expected threshold for their interaction with their surrounding medium, which may indicate the presence of relativistic turbulence in the surrounding medium.

We are examining the bipartite vertex splitting problem, which involves determining the minimum number of edges to add to a bipartite graph so that it becomes a graph with a specific property related to its adjacency matrix being non-singular. We develop a new approach that uses parameterized algorithms based on the number of vertices in a given subset of the graph's edges. Specifically, we present a new method that utilizes a bipartite graph parameterized by the number of vertices in a given subset of the edges, and show that recognizing graphs whose adjacency matrix is non-singular can be done efficiently using this parameterized approach. We also investigate the relationship between this parameter and another parameter, k, which represents the minimum number of vertices in a given subset of the graph's edges. We discuss the implications of this relationship and its relevance to other problems related to vertex splitting in different types of graphs. We present a new approach that utilizes a bipartite graph parameterized by the number of vertices in a given subset of the graph's edges, and show that recognizing graphs whose adjacency matrix is non-singular can be done efficiently using this parameterized approach. We also consider the case where the graph is required to be undirected, and show that this problem is also solvable using our proposed method. We discuss the limitations of our approach and its relevance to other problems related to vertex splitting in different types of graphs.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various visual recognition tasks, but their practical application is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data across all classes. One effective strategy to overcome this challenge is incremental learning, which allows for learning from new data in an unbalanced manner. However, this approach often results in catastrophic forgetting of previously learned classes and skewed decision boundaries due to the skewed nature of the data. To mitigate these issues, researchers have explored different calibration methods to adjust the model's decision boundaries and output probabilities. This review paper provides a comprehensive analysis of different calibration methods applied to visual recognition tasks in an unbalanced incremental learning setting, with a focus on temperature scaling, regression-based approaches, and boundary adjustment techniques. The results show that these methods can improve the model's accuracy and probability calibration, but they also come with trade-offs in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. The authors believe that the findings of this review will contribute to the ongoing research in unbalanced incremental learning and help guide future research directions.

This paper presents key advancements in our thruster-supported bipedal locomotion framework. Initially, we employ a hybrid dynamics model to precisely capture the behavior of a bipedal robot utilizing thruster-based propulsion. This approach allows for more accurate control of the robot's movement by accounting for propulsion impulses and potential impacts. Subsequently, we develop a novel optimization algorithm, building upon the Fast Convergence Program (FCP), to efficiently solve the robot's dynamic motion problem. This method achieves near-optimal solutions with significantly reduced computational time. Furthermore, we refine the algorithm to mitigate errors resulting from simulated-to-real discrepancies, ensuring smoother and more reliable robot performance. Experimental validation on a physical robot demonstrates the efficacy of these innovations.

Let $R$ be an integral domain within a field $K$, with a total residue map defined as $\lambda: K^* \to R$. This implies that for any element $x$ in the field $K$, there exists an element $r$ in the domain $R$ such that $\lambda(x) = r$ mod $R$. This condition is equivalent to stating that the pair $(R, \lambda)$ forms a valued ring, with $R$ being an ideal-valued domain. This research explores the characteristics of such domains and offers a classification of those that are unique factorization domains. Additionally, it provides a new proof for a theorem by Fontana and Ribbe, showing that such domains which are Prufer multiplicative domains of finite character with a discrete value group, are characterized by having a finite set of maximal ideals with residue fields that are algebraically closed.

Modern CPUs are highly optimized for specific types of computations, but this optimization comes at the cost of increased power consumption. To overcome this limitation, we introduce HyperDegrade, a novel technique that intentionally degrades CPU performance by lowering clock frequencies. Our research reveals that lowering CPU clock frequencies to a small fraction of their maximum efficiency yields significant improvements in energy consumption. Specifically, we found that reducing CPU frequencies to between 10-30% of their maximum efficiency results in up to 10x energy savings. To demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade, we developed a system that automatically identifies the optimal frequency range for a given application and applies the technique to a variety of workloads, including web browsers, media players, and scientific simulations. Our technique is implemented as a system-level modification, requiring no changes to the application code. Overall, HyperDegrade provides a simple yet effective means of reducing energy consumption on modern computing systems.

We investigate the impact of supersymmetry on resolving the discrepancy between the Standard Model prediction and the experimental measurement of the muon's magnetic moment anomaly. Assuming the Higgs boson is not part of a complex superfield, we identify the most significant supersymmetric contributions to this anomaly and determine the necessary mass scale for the lightest electroweak superpartners to resolve the observed discrepancy. This solution is then used to estimate the expected supersymmetric contributions to dark matter scattering off nucleons in direct detection experiments.

A method for determining the CP-violating phase $\gamma$ from $B^\pm \to \bar{D}^{*0} D^0$ and $B^\pm \to D^{-} D^0$ decays, utilizing the spin of the $D^{*0}$, has been presented. By using a tagged $B$ meson and reconstructing the $\bar{D}^{*0}$ and $D^0$ via $K^0_S \pi^0$ and $K^+ K^-$ decays, respectively, an interference pattern emerges from the $D^0$ decays, which can be used to extract a single angle from the $B$ decay. It is shown that a more precise measurement of $\gamma$ can be achieved with a more precise $D^0$ reconstruction, and a measurement of $\gamma = 6.8^{+1.4}_{-1.3} \pm 0.3$ degrees from a sample of 1000 $B$ decays, is presented. Furthermore, an estimate of the achievable precision with a full dataset from the LHCb experiment is provided.

We propose a novel operation, called disentanglement, applicable to both closed classical and welded links. This operation differs from the standard link fusion process. By combining these operations, we can derive an essential characteristic for welded links known as the Hopf invariant. Notably, this makes the set of welded links non-commutative. When using only disentanglement, we can establish a formula for changing from one representation to another, known as the Markov 2 move. This leads to a conclusion that the set of links is now fully described when considering both our disentanglement operation and the Markov 2 move. We also explore the implications of this finding on the study of the knot group.

A tropical curve's rational function semifield has been shown to correspond biologically to its amplitude matrix semifield, and we've established a connection between this semifield and the curve's tropical structure, specifically its genus and decomposition into edges and vertices. Given a tropical curve within a rational toric variety, we can construct a semifield of rational functions that reflects the curve's tropical amplitude matrix semifield. This function semifield can be generated by a finite set of functions over the curve's semifield of tropical series.

We've discovered that the combination of the box move and the Fox-Hatcher move results in an equivalent expression for the third-order clasp in knot knot polynomials. The proposed clasp move's effect on the Jones polynomial can be broken down into a specific formula, allowing us to derive a new, general method for producing 3-tangle equivalences. This new method enables us to establish that a particular Vassiliev invariant, known as the Gassner representation, can be expressed using its value from specific, pre-determined 2-tangles. Additionally, we've applied this general method to prove that the third-order Vassiliev knot invariant derived from the Kauffman polynomial is equal to a linear combination of specific, pre-determined invariants.

The new data from the KATRIN experiment, which set a precise upper limit on electron antineutrino mass squared of 0.8 eV/c^2 at a 90% confidence level, has significant implications for understanding the absolute scale of neutrino mass. To better understand this data, researchers have applied the Dalley-Weisskopf method to analyze the continuous electron spectrum from tritium beta decay, yielding a lower limit on neutrino mass of 0.65 x 10^-2 eV/c^2. To address experimental limitations, a more accurate calculation of the molecular final-state distribution was performed, which could improve the lower limit on neutrino mass to 0.59 x 10^-2 eV/c^2. This research also provides a theoretical framework for interpreting future experiments, such as the HOLMES and HOLSTEN projects, which aim to further investigate the absolute scale of neutrino mass.

Matrix multiplication is a fundamental operation in linear algebra with numerous applications in areas like computer graphics, machine learning, and data analysis. This study compares the performance of sequential (CPU) and parallel (GPU) matrix multiplication approaches for large matrices. By implementing both methods in C, we tested them on matrices of varying sizes (100x100 to 2000x2000) and measured execution time. Results indicate that GPU-based parallel multiplication outperforms CPU sequential multiplication for large matrices due to its ability to process multiple calculations simultaneously.

A novel algorithm is proposed for synchronizing a group of robots on a regular lattice to a target configuration, based on their shared knowledge of the lattice structure. The proposed method leverages a specific communication and computation strategy, resulting in predictable message transmission and local state changes, ultimately synchronizing the robots to the desired configuration within a time frame of O(n) messages, where 'n' represents the total number of robots. This algorithm is optimal in terms of message efficiency and represents the first solution for multi-robot synchronization on regular graphs. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the impossibility of achieving synchronization under the given constraints for any graph with more than three nodes, when the robots have no knowledge of the graph structure. The proposed algorithm is also shown to be a unique optimal solution for synchronization on regular graphs with more than two nodes, under the given constraints. The paper includes a proof of the uniqueness of the proposed algorithm. The proposed algorithm is shown to be applicable to a broader class of graphs, including those that are not regular, and the results are discussed in the context of graph size and robot distribution. As precision measurements at particle accelerators advance, the need for refined theoretical predictions increases, particularly in infrared-sensitive scattering processes. These processes, heavily influenced by multiple emissions of low-energy particles, significantly alter cross-sections and observable patterns. To address this, novel theoretical approaches are being explored to account for the impact of multiple soft and collinear emissions. This paper reviews the results of amplitude-based resummation, a method that effectively captures the impact of such emissions, while also discussing its limitations and challenges.

This section outlines the difficulties encountered by individuals who have been targeted by privacy breaches in a VFL system. The challenges faced by attackers in VFL settings are outlined, and a framework for evaluating VFL assaults is presented. The proposed evaluation framework is employed to assess current VFL methods, revealing their vulnerabilities to various attacks. The results obtained from these evaluations are documented.

Kernel methods are widely used in machine learning for their effectiveness in tackling complex, non-linear data patterns. However, they are often computationally expensive, especially when dealing with large datasets. We propose a novel approach to estimating non-linear functions efficiently, utilizing a randomized fourier feature mapping. Our method utilizes a subset of training data to estimate the distribution of a non-linear function, and subsequently, develops randomized features to approximate this function. We demonstrate the theoretical underpinnings of our approach and compare our data-dependent kernel method to existing random kitchen sink and fourier feature methods on multiple datasets.

The primary objective of this research is to establish a new capability in which any group that acts on sets as a direct product of two components can be seamlessly incorporated into a wreath product group with the same number of times it is producted. This achievement is made while maintaining the direct product structure and the original action of the two component groups. Our solution leverages the decomposition of groups under the Cartesian product and utilizes existing theorems to prove our claim.

This research extends a previous finding by Y. Ni, which demonstrated the impossibility of a certain type of hypersurface in a higher-dimensional space, specifically one with a particular type of curvature. Building on this, we establish that a certain type of hypersurface, defined by a constant mean curvature, cannot exist under a more stringent curvature requirement. Furthermore, we establish the non-existence of another type of hypersurface, which has a specific type of curvature and embedding properties, under a broader range of conditions.

Three-dimensional cardiac MRI (MRIc) is a highly effective imaging technique for assessing cardiac anatomy and function. However, its high cost and lengthy acquisition time hinder its use in patients with rare congenital heart diseases (CHDs). Cardiac MRI can be utilized to evaluate cardiac function in these patients and supplement echocardiography, which may not be suitable for visualizing complex cardiac structures in CHD patients. Utilizing automated segmentation techniques can facilitate the analysis of MRIc images, but current methods often struggle to accurately segment complex cardiac structures in patients with CHDs. A study was conducted to evaluate the transferability of a U-Net-based cardiac MRI segmentation method to three rare CHD cases, in comparison to manual segmentation and visual assessment. The study found that while the automated method produced satisfactory results in some cases, it was unable to accurately segment complex cardiac structures in others. The study suggests that more sophisticated training models and data augmentation techniques may be necessary to improve the accuracy of automated segmentation in patients with CHDs. The study highlights the importance of developing reliable automated segmentation methods to facilitate the utilization of cardiac MRI in patients with CHDs.

The proposed degradation models capture the spatial variation in material properties within a broader class of heterogeneous and rapidly changing materials. 
These models express the elasticity modulus as a gradient of a scalar function, providing significant benefits in terms of numerical efficiency and data management. 
By utilizing these properties, the boundary condition can be accurately approximated with high-order accuracy using only interior information, thus eliminating the need for extensive boundary mesh refinement. 
Furthermore, this approach enables the use of enriched basis functions to accurately capture boundary layer effects, ultimately reducing computational costs.

A new type of wireless network that uses SWIPT technology has been explored, where some devices can both send and receive data, and also convert unused data into electrical energy. To understand the benefits of SWIPT, a problem was formulated to find the best way to allocate bandwidth in a network that supports multiple types of data services. This problem was then simplified by focusing on networks that only have one type of server. Three different methods for allocating bandwidth were analyzed, including systems that have one type of server and those that have multiple servers that can send and receive data. To solve the complex problems that arise, a new algorithm was developed using an integer programming technique. This algorithm was tested on a simulated network and found to be effective in allocating bandwidth. The results showed that SWIPT technology can improve the efficiency of a single-server network by up to 25%, but has little effect on networks that only have one type of server.

The proposed approach, All Objects Attention (AOA), addresses the limitation of existing methods that focus on a limited number of objects in images. Unlike these techniques, our method leverages an attention mechanism to consider all detectable objects, enhancing the model's ability to handle complex queries. Our experiments demonstrate significant performance gains over current focal image detection models and current multi-object detection techniques, particularly in scenarios with multiple target objects. Notably, our approach achieves comparable accuracy to the best-performing baselines while requiring fewer detectable objects. Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengzheng0605/focal_image_detection.

This research explores the conditions under which a specific subgroup of a given probability distribution, such as the Weibull or Gumbel distribution, can be accurately modeled by a more complex, mixed distribution like a mixture of Weibull or Gaussian models. We have established precise conditions for when these simpler, conditional distributions can arise from their respective more complex, mixed counterparts. Notably, we found that a Gamma-conditioned Weibull distribution cannot be accurately represented by a mixture of Gaussian models, and a Gaussian-conditioned Weibull distribution cannot be accurately represented by a mixture of Gamma models. These research findings have significant implications for the field of machine learning, particularly in the area of mixture models.

This paper introduces a novel approach to Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) using a pre-trained Chinese gloss BERT (CGlossBERT) model.  As part of the innovative Onomastic Paradox paradigm, researchers are exploring methods to enhance NLP models' performance on WSD tasks by leveraging human-annotated metadata.  To this end, we propose a pre-trained Chinese model that incorporates bilingual glosses into its architecture, enabling it to process and utilize metadata during the inference stage.  We experimentally evaluate CGlossBERT's effectiveness on the MSRA-WSD dataset, and the results indicate a notable improvement in F1 scores compared to the baseline model.  We believe our work provides a pioneering framework for NLP tasks within the Onomastic Paradox paradigm and sets the stage for further research and development.

To effectively convey complex real-world tasks, such as cooking or assembling furniture, through multiple modalities, comprehensive guidebooks provide an excellent example. These documents employ a range of sensory inputs, including visual images, written instructions, and sequential steps, to convey procedural knowledge. By analyzing guidebooks across various domains, we can extract and understand the underlying principles of multimodal procedural knowledge. Our approach involves using sequential learning techniques to process the sequential nature of guidebook steps, resulting in a model capable of representing and predicting future steps based on past experiences. Our research findings suggest that incorporating a diverse range of modalities, such as visual images and written instructions, enables a more accurate and efficient representation of procedural knowledge. Additionally, our results suggest that the structure and organization of guidebook steps play a crucial role in representing multimodal procedural knowledge.

A previous study proposed that the avalanche-magnitude distribution for hierarchical lattice models follows a power law, but this conclusion was based on a limited definition of an avalanche event. A new definition has been developed, and its implications have been examined for both hierarchical lattices and Cayley trees. A direct relationship has been established between these two definitions of an avalanche event in the context of hierarchical lattices, and Monte Carlo simulations have been conducted to determine the new avalanche-magnitude distribution for Cayley trees. The results show that the new distribution also follows a power law, confirming the original conclusion. A theoretical derivation has also been developed to support these findings.

This paper extends the classical Airy differential equation y''-xy=0 to y''-xy=x^ny, where n is any real number, and develops an orthogonal system of "Airy-type" polynomials. Building on this, we examine the special case where n=-2, and demonstrate the existence of "Laguerre-type" and "Hermite" polynomials. Additionally, this paper provides an asymptotic analysis for large values of the degree, and an explicit formula for the coefficients of the potential function using Gamma functions.

To enhance the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies, we propose a novel technique called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer. This method leverages the non-reciprocal nature of the Sagnac effect to increase the optical power circulating within the detector's arms. By manipulating the properties of the circulating light, this technique can overcome the shot noise limitations typically associated with traditional interferometric detectors. The concept is demonstrated with existing technology, and the design is optimized to minimize thermal noise, ultimately improving the sensitivity of the detector by a factor of approximately 1.5 to 2 compared to standard setups.

Next-generation massive MIMO systems are expected to significantly enhance mobile broadband services through XL-MIMO technology, which involves deploying massive MIMO arrays on large surfaces. This technology creates new challenges due to the complex array layout and the resulting multi-path interference. In this paper, we investigate an uplink random access protocol for XL-MIMO systems, where access is controlled by non-overlapping time intervals. Our analysis of user distribution and base station array geometry reveals that some base stations may have no access opportunities, and we derive an expression for the non-intersecting visibility region. We also propose future research directions to address these findings.

This research paper examines the potential of substructures within protoplanetary disks to be observed in dust continuum images, specifically focusing on structures generated by vertical shear instability. To make accurate predictions about detectability, we utilize 3D radiative transfer simulations to simulate observations at millimeter wavelengths. Our analysis reveals that the level of substructure visibility in these images is influenced by the wavelength of observation, as well as the characteristics of the disk, such as its temperature and scattering properties. We predict that the substructures in the simulated disk will be most prominent at a wavelength of 1.2 millimeters, with a maximum amplitude of about 10 percent. Furthermore, we estimate that the structures will be most detectable at a wavelength of 3 millimeters with a maximum amplitude of about 5 percent. We also predict that the structures will be detectable at a wavelength of 0.87 millimeters with a maximum amplitude of about 2 percent.
