Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various applications, particularly in pattern recognition tasks. Despite their widespread adoption, comprehending the underlying mechanisms of these sophisticated models remains a significant challenge. This paper provides an in-depth explanation of the current state-of-the-art methods for analyzing and interpreting DNNs, with a focus on their comprehensibility and explanatory power. Additionally, this survey highlights the role of visualizations in facilitating the interpretation of DNNs, with a specific emphasis on their ability to convey information effectively. Furthermore, this paper categorizes explanation methods into three distinct groups: post-hoc, intrinsic, and global, with each category offering unique insights into the behavior and performance of DNNs. This comprehensive analysis of comprehending and explaining DNNs is accompanied by a range of visualizations designed to facilitate understanding and facilitate further research in this critical area.

Recent observations of young stars in the process of forming have shown that some of them are spinning at an unusually fast rate, which is contrary to expectations. This is because the angular momentum is thought to be efficiently transferred out of the system, but the observations suggest that angular momentum transfer may not be as effective as previously thought. In a new study, we found evidence in the spectral data of a young star named V823 Aur that suggests the transfer of angular momentum is being effectively managed by a disk surrounding the star. We also found evidence in the spectra of other young stars, such as V1645 Mon and V4046 Sco, that suggests they may be consuming a planet which is transferring its angular momentum to the star. These findings suggest that the unexpectedly fast rotation of some young stars may not be a result of inefficient angular momentum transfer, but rather a result of the transfer of angular momentum from an accreting planet.

The escalating spread of false information on social media poses significant challenges in maintaining public awareness and trust. Although numerous techniques have been developed to detect fake news, most of them focus on text-based information and overlook the influence of accompanying images. Our research addresses this limitation by creating an innovative approach called MetaFND, which leverages both textual and visual data to identify false news. We introduce a novel emergent representation learning framework that allows the model to automatically infer missing information from available data. By integrating this with meta-learning, our approach efficiently adapts to new instances of false news using limited labeled data. Our experiments demonstrate that MetaFND outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness.

This research examines the cyclic transport equation in n-dimensional space, where the velocity field is the difference between the cyclic shift of a scalar function and the original function. We've identified conditions under which the equation's solution, given compact initial data, maintains a specific property known as C^r decay. The study also considers the case of dimension two, where we can guarantee that the solution preserves this characteristic for infinitely many iterations. The work builds upon previous findings by D. Serre and the author, expanding on their results regarding the preservation of solution regularity.

This research focuses on a discrete time system that manages updating devices based on a status refresh model. The study aims to minimize the average information quality loss, taking into account both server service rates and transmission success probabilities. The paper derives the exact formula for average information quality loss, develops a method to find the optimal policy, and provides a more efficient algorithm to speed up the process. The time requirements of the original and new algorithms are compared, demonstrating the benefits of the improved approach. The algorithm is also adaptable to other types of arrival distributions and service rate constraints, and the algorithm's process is visually illustrated with flow charts for better understanding.

The research investigates the construction of quasi-bialgebras from set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation, utilizing a specified algebra A and an invertible scalar c. Key components include a linear map Delta and an invertible element f within A x A, which satisfy specific axioms. Notably, the focus is on placing the algebra A within the context of a monoidal category, with the requirement that the category be equivalent to the category of modules over an algebra.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices and beams have gained significant attention due to their ability to eliminate range ambiguity and side lobes in radar systems. Building on this achievement, research has sought to develop Golay complementary structures with higher numbers of range bins, phases, and beams. This research presents novel Golay complementary structures using combination and tensor product methods, specifically combining BCCM and GCM to create GCA with twice the elements of original structures, and using the Kronecker product to generate GCA with twice the number of range bins, three times the numbers of phases, and three times the numbers of beams. A new algorithm is also proposed to design GCM with doubled elements, and the proposed designs are verified through a practical example.

Quantum interference in conducting molecules is a well-established phenomenon, but in silicon-based molecules, interference patterns are influenced by the atomic valley degree of freedom, which is absent in group-IV carbons. By using scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigated the electronic properties of silicon molecules placed on an indium antimonide surface, where the interference patterns are affected by both the atomic valley and electron spin. We observed that swapping a single atomic silicon atom for its neighboring valley state can swap the spins of the molecule's current, a phenomenon known as valley interference spin swapping. This effect is not seen in group-IV carbons due to their different electronic properties. Our findings provide a pathway for controlling interference patterns in silicon molecules and open up new possibilities for scanning probe applications in quantum computing.

Complex systems science is an intricate discipline that spans multiple disciplines, characterized by a vast number of components and intricate interactions. These systems often exhibit dynamic behavior that is highly sensitive to initial conditions, making them difficult to predict. Despite significant theoretical and empirical progress, a unified framework for studying complex systems remains elusive. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of complex systems dynamics and introduces a novel framework for their analysis. This framework integrates graph neural networks with dynamic modeling and generative modeling, enabling a unified approach to modeling complex systems. It leverages graph neural networks to model system interactions and employs a conditional approach to model their dynamic behavior. This framework is demonstrated through a case study of the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting its potential for real-world applications.

We introduce a novel family of partition functions $\xi_n$ and demonstrate their utility in homotopy theory, specifically in determining the rational homotopy groups of iterated loop spaces of spheres and the stable homotopy groups of spheres. Our approach builds upon the foundational work of Kuhn, Rezk, and Tang, offering a more streamlined and conceptually simpler proof. Additionally, we employ our method to derive new outcomes for the homotopy spheres when considering iterated suspensions up to $n-1$.

The rapid development of motor vehicles has led to a significant increase in traffic accidents, resulting in severe injuries to many individuals. One of the most common injuries is traumatic brain injury (TBI), which poses a major threat to human life. To address this issue, it is crucial to develop accurate traffic injury prediction systems that can provide timely medical assistance to injured individuals. However, generating realistic injury data remains a significant challenge due to its complex and irregular distribution. In this study, we propose a novel data augmentation approach called Biphasic Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (BPAVE) for creating realistic injury data. Our proposed method achieves an F1 score of 0.75, outperforming existing data generation techniques. The improved performance of BPAVE is attributed to its two-stage generation process, which allows for the creation of high-quality data by combining the strengths of Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

We have investigated quantum nonlocality in multipartite scenarios, specifically in d-dimensional systems comprising products of unextendible product bases (UPBs). We've found that nonlocality can be demonstrated using a biseparable state for any such set, and we've found the minimum number of qudits required to exhibit robust quantum nonlocality in all possible UPB-based sets is 9. Furthermore, we've shown the minimum number of qudits required to exhibit robust quantum nonlocality in all possible d-dimensional UPB-based sets is 13 for dimensions d greater than or equal to 5. We've also found the nonlocality can be demonstrated using a wide range of positive operator-valued measurements, and we've found the nonlocality can be robust for a wide range of measurement noises in some specific UPB-based sets.

The Complete Safe Coordination Algorithm (CSCA) effectively manages the complex task of synchronizing multiple telescopes to conduct extensive astronomical surveys. Its capability to handle multiple objectives and distribute telescopes efficiently makes it particularly suitable for large-scale survey projects. In this study, we tested the CSCA by simulating the distribution of seven telescopes across three types of surveys: deep, wide, and wide with varying depths. The results showed that the CSCC can successfully coordinate the allocation of telescopes to optimize the scientific output of the telescopes. The results also provided valuable insights into the optimal number of telescopes required to achieve the best possible scientific output. The data obtained from this study can inform future projects, such as the completion of the SDSS-V, about the best way to distribute astrobots to maximize the scientific output of the project.

The original GP 2 compiler has been significantly improved by incorporating the OpenCL 1.2 front end, which has been developed using a top-down approach based on the GP 1.2 grammar. This enhancement enables GP 2 to be compiled directly from OpenCL 1.2 source code, bypassing the need for an intermediate language. Notably, this development was achieved without modifying GP 2's own grammar, as it shares a compatible structure with OpenCL 1.2. This compatibility stems from the fact that GP 1.2 was itself derived from OpenCL 1.1, which in turn was based on GP 1.1.

To address the issue of limited labeled data in medical image analysis, learning robust image representations is crucial. Despite various approaches, there is no universally accepted method for feature extraction. In this study, we introduce a novel framework for learning images features using contrastive learning, which can handle both supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios. Our framework is designed to handle diverse applications, including image classification, segmentation, and registration, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through comprehensive experiments on medical image analysis tasks.

A graph is considered star normal if its automorphism group acts transitively on its vertex set while having a regular, non-primitive action on the graph's point set. In 2019, Li and Praeger initiated the search for star normal graphs that possess a specific twisted wreath symmetry. This paper presents an infinite series of such graphs, proving that for certain prime numbers, there exist star normal graphs with a twisted wreath symmetry. Additionally, these graphs are the second known family of star normal graphs that possess a twisted primitive group structure.

Working with categorical data in machine learning models is complicated by the need to account for multiple levels within each variable. This study focuses on improving the Lasso and Group Lasso methods for handling high-dimensional categorical data. To achieve this, we introduce an algorithm that combines the cyclic coordinate descent method with the active set strategy, which is particularly effective for the Group Lasso method. When dealing with a large number of variables, we also suggest an alternative approach that incorporates the proximal gradient method. Our proposed algorithm was tested against existing solutions in various group sparsity settings and demonstrated superior performance. Additionally, we applied the algorithm to a real-world dataset from the 2010 UK census, where it successfully identified key socio-economic factors associated with changes in population size.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved remarkable success, 
however, their ability to accurately incorporate structured data remains limited. 
While some methods can utilize the global patterns in language models' language 
skills, they are unable to effectively apply this ability to the specific 
injections of structured knowledge. This research proposes a novel method called 
SKILL, which utilizes the language models' ability to learn and apply structured 
data through a two-stage process. In the first stage, a compact structure is 
created to represent the data, and in the second stage, this data is injected 
into the language models by training them to apply this structure. Our method 
achieves a 90% reduction in training parameters compared to traditional methods, 
and outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches on multiple benchmarks 
including GSM8K, AR, and the Entity Linking task. Our code is available at 
https://github.com/ChenZongyi1999/SKILL.

This paper introduces a nonlocal diffusion model with a fixed small-scale parameter, and derives convergent approximations for a solution as this parameter decreases. The conclusion of the analysis reveals that the solution approaches the solution of a singular perturbation differential equation, and our proof is based on obtaining a uniform bound and deriving convergence estimates in a specific C^1,δ space. These estimates are of particular interest due to their applicability to the study of nonlocal models. The framework employed in the paper serves as a useful tool for understanding nonlocal models with consistent local limits.

The paper provides an overview of the foundational steps for a systematic approach to removing a specific type of singularity, namely an Eisenstein pole, from a broader class of automorphic distributions, involving multiple representations of $GL(n)$. This method has significant implications for the Woodberry-Tadi\'c theorem and related results.

Neurodegenerative disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, are characterized by the deterioration of specific brain areas and the subsequent loss of motor control. This loss of motor control is often attributed to the malfunction of basal ganglia circuits, which are influenced by dopamine deficiency. However, the root cause of this dopamine deficiency is not fully understood. To gain a deeper insight into this issue, researchers have turned to computational models that can simulate the complex interactions within the brain. In this study, we have developed a novel computational model that can accurately replicate the activity of individual neurons and neural circuits in a Parkinson's-diseased marmoset monkey brain. This model is based on a comprehensive dataset of cortical neurons and their synaptic connections, which was collected using two-photon calcium imaging and whole-cell patch-clamp recordings. To account for the unique properties of marmoset neurons, the model incorporates a biophysically accurate description of neuronal dynamics, which was derived from an existing open-source dataset. The model's performance was validated through a series of experiments, which demonstrated its ability to accurately replicate the activity of neurons in a Parkinson's-diseased marmoset monkey brain. This study marks a significant advancement in the field of computational neuroscience, as it paves the way for the development of more sophisticated brain models that can accurately replicate the activity of the human brain.

This paper introduces a novel approach to efficiently rendering line joins from vector maps at a scaled level, utilizing an algorithm that translates path data into scaled coordinates and leverages an inverse transformation to generate corresponding screen coordinates. This method allows lines to maintain their original dimensions while being rendered at a scaled level. The proposed solution is an innovative anti-aliasing technique for lines that are joined in paths, offering a more efficient alternative to existing methods.

We present initial findings from observations of nine extremely luminous galaxies using the KOOLS-IFU on the Seimei Telescope. These observations were made at redshifts less than 0.04, and the galaxies span a range of distances and orientations. By analyzing the integral field data, we identified emission lines in the optical spectrum and created velocity maps. Preliminary results show that the galaxies have rotational velocities of up to 200 km/s, and their gas kinematics are generally well-ordered. These results are a step towards a more comprehensive study of galaxy dynamics and gas flows in extreme luminosity galaxies.

The multivariate interpolation operator utilizing a positive definite function of the Euclidean distance can achieve second-order accuracy for sufficiently smooth functions, based on a dense and unstructured node set in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The issue with standard RBF interpolation lies in its tendency to produce oscillations and node-reversal phenomena, leading to a lack of shape preservation. To address this problem, an improved interpolation scheme has been proposed, incorporating an auxiliary factor that ensures the preservation of data shape and results in piecewise $C^1$-smoothness for piecewise quadratic behavior. The proposed auxiliary function utilizes a novel transcendental function of the Euclidean distance, specifically tailored to meet certain criteria within a bounded domain. The new transcendental function offers greater flexibility and broader applicability compared to existing alternatives. Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate the scheme's desirable properties and confirm its quadratic convergence rate. The scheme's ability to preserve convex hulls and produce smooth results is also demonstrated through selected examples.

Accurate weather forecasting is crucial for public safety and the prevention of property damage. Conventional weather prediction methods, such as numerical weather prediction and statistical weather prediction, are often too costly or unreliable to provide real-time, localized weather information. Machine learning-based approaches have been explored as a means to predict real-time weather, but they are typically trained on limited datasets that may not be representative of the target population. This limitation is compounded by the lack of publicly available datasets that include diverse weather conditions. To address this issue, we have created a comprehensive dataset that encompasses six distinct weather categories, including clear skies, scattered clouds, overcast skies, rain, snow, and hail. This dataset is designed to facilitate the development and testing of weather prediction models. We have also explored data augmentation techniques to enhance the dataset's diversity and improve model performance. Our experiments have shown that convolutional neural network-based models can achieve high levels of accuracy in predicting weather conditions, with a top model achieving 90% accuracy. This work paves the way for future advancements in weather prediction and could have significant implications for public safety and the prevention of property damage.

Non-stationary noise removal from speech signals is a significant challenge in speech enhancement. This paper introduces a novel architecture, Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks to effectively learn temporal dependencies and local features. The DPCRN model is specifically designed to handle single-channel noisy speech data and was tested on two widely used datasets, Aishell-2 and Voicebank-DEMOS. Experimental results show that the proposed network outperforms existing convolutional neural network-based speech enhancement models, achieving a 0.5 dB improvement in Word Error Rate on the Aishell-2 dataset.

This combination is then applied to a model of the universe that includes dark energy, dark matter, a specific type of matter halo, and a neutrino fluid. This model is then compared to real-world observations of galaxy clusters to understand how it affects the size of these halos at a critical turning point. This critical point is determined by the balance between the force of gravity and the outward pressure from the hot gas within the halo. The study finds that the combination of the gravity theory and a specific mass for neutrinos can significantly affect the size of these halos at this critical point. This study aims to develop a two-fluid model for Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection, with a view to eventually applying multi-fluid modelling to atmospheric convection. Initially, we used a single-fluid model to simulate the atmospheric boundary layer, with and without the influence of latent heat release. We then combined these models and simulated convection with rising bubbles and cold water. We found that the two-fluid model successfully simulated convection, with the bubbles rising and the cold water sinking as expected. However, further development is needed to accurately model air bubbles and ice in the atmosphere.

A quantum network's success depends on maintaining the coherence of its components.  We've studied how entanglement between two separate atoms, initially in a state of zero correlation, evolves over time due to interaction with their local cavities under the Jaynes-Cummings model.  Our analysis shows that certain parameters can lead to a sudden decrease in atomic entanglement, resulting from the atoms becoming entangled with their respective cavities.  Interestingly, this effect can be controlled by adjusting the atoms' initial energy levels.  Our findings also indicate that increasing the atomic energy levels can delay the onset of atomic sudden death.  Moreover, we've shown that an external magnetic field can influence the occurrence of atomic sudden death. The CMS experiment at the LHC has been upgraded to accommodate the increased luminosity of Phase-1, which has led to the installation of a new pixel detector consisting of approximately 850,000 sensors. This upgrade has been facilitated by the development of new systems, including the readout, power, and alignment infrastructure. The new sensors are organized into layers, with the outer two layers being "bar" layers and the inner three layers being "blade" layers. The reconstruction of the pixel pilot blades is a critical component of the overall detector performance, which is being examined in this paper. The authors present the design and performance of the pixel pilot blade reconstruction system, which is being used to reconstruct tracks in the innermost region of the upgraded pixel detector. The performance of the track reconstruction is evaluated using data collected during proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, and the results show that the track reconstruction efficiency and resolution are within the expected ranges. The results also show that the track impact parameter resolution is within the expected range, which is critical for the identification of long-lived particles. The authors discuss the implications of these results for the overall performance of the upgraded pixel detector.

Our study presents a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation for the SU(2) gluonium scalar susceptibility, utilizing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral form of the SU(2) gluonium scalar two-point correlation function. By analyzing lattice QCD data for the SU(2) gluonium scalar susceptibility and a suitable set of hadronic states, we derive the spectral function within a specific energy range. Additionally, we estimate the SU(2) SUSY QCD SUSY pions' contribution to the SU(2) gluonium scalar spectral function.

Social media platforms, particularly Twitter, have become a valuable source of real-time public opinion data. This paper outlines a sentiment analysis system that utilizes the Twitter API to collect and analyze users' status updates, incorporating natural language processing techniques and an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network. By training the LSTM model on a dataset of labeled tweets, the system successfully classifies the sentiment of each tweet as positive, negative, or neutral. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through the visualization of sentiment trends over time, with the LSTMMicroFramework as the underlying technology.

A linear charge-adding process is used to derive the shade thermodynamics of a specific type of black hole in anti-de Sitter space, characterized by being non-linearly charged and lacking rotational movement. The study reveals that the thermodynamic behavior of this black hole changes significantly at the point where the linearity of its charge is no longer maintained, with the shade free energy showing the potential to represent phase transitions within this system.

The primary objective of this research is to provide a comprehensive explanation of the unique features of the universal quantum evolution of a single qubit, based on the Wigner function and its subsequent transformation. This study focuses on the ability of quantum tomography to effectively track the onset of entanglement and synchronization within a system. By utilizing a specific model of a damped two-level system, we have demonstrated that the evolution of its density matrix can lead to the emergence of entanglement and synchronization, even in the absence of initial entanglement. Furthermore, we have identified a critical threshold in the entanglement of formation, which occurs when the local entanglement of the qubit surpasses a certain value. This threshold is found to be directly related to the onset of synchronization within the system.

Building a dialogue system that adheres to a particular role while maintaining openness to other topics is a challenging task. This task is particularly difficult due to the limited availability of data that captures the nuances of human conversations. Current approaches that rely on closed systems and predefined topic boundaries are insufficient for this open-domain challenge. In this study, we explore a novel specification-based method for defining role specifications, which can be used to describe the desired specification of a particular role. We then develop a large-scale dataset containing over 100,000 conversations that capture the essence of a particular role, which can be used to train an open-domain dialogue model that adheres to the specified role. Our experiments demonstrate that our specification-based method is effective in constructing a large-scale dataset that captures the essence of a particular role, which in turn leads to an open-domain dialogue system that exhibits superior performance in terms of role adherence and naturalness of conversation.

Evaluating pest management methods is a complex task due to the variability of agricultural data. To address this challenge, we developed a robust regression approach that mitigates the effects of extreme values, which are common in such datasets. We tested our method on strawberry disease management data, comparing it to traditional techniques like quantile regression and ordinary least squares. The results showed that our robust approach effectively identified key factors influencing treatment efficacy, particularly in cases where data variability was high.

Creating a 360-degree virtual tourism video involves capturing a 360-degree video and creating a perspective prediction model that can accurately estimate the viewer's orientation within the scene. This task is crucial for enhancing user interaction with 360-degree videos. However, the lack of explicit user guidance on their orientation can make this process challenging. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages subtitle information to assist in perspective prediction. By incorporating the textual information from subtitles, our method can effectively predict the user's orientation and provide a more immersive virtual tourism experience. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately predicting perspective and providing a more engaging 360-degree virtual tourism experience.

We introduce a novel tensor network structure known as the locally precise tensor network (LPTN), which effectively represents thermal states and system behavior under thermal conditions. The LSTM architecture enables the precise modeling of both short and long-distance interactions, as well as the application of thermal conditions, leading to a successful simulation of physical phenomena. Our simulations demonstrate the accuracy of the LPTM in modeling thermal correlations, entropy, and entropy production in thermal scenarios, including the thermal version of the Aharonov-Casher effect. Furthermore, the entropy production is also applicable to the non-thermal case. The results indicate that the LPTN is a powerful tool for studying thermal quantum systems.

We propose a decoupling approach for complex systems by decoupling their components from one another and from their surroundings. We decouple the system into independent, simple parts that can be analyzed separately. We propose a method of decoupling by evaluating the limited impact of each part. We suggest measuring the limited effect of each component relative to a specific scale. We propose a new approach to decoupling by assessing the limited efficacy of each component. We show that our method can be applied to a range of examples, including a two-dimensional Ising model, a two-dimensional lattice gas, and a two-dimensional Potts model.

We investigate anisotropic $p$-capacitance in R^n and anisotropic Weyl-Minkowski inequality in R^n. In anisotropic space R^n, the $p$-capacitance of a ring formed by two compact sets K and E, where K is contained within E, can be minimized when the ring is composed of an ellipsoid and its corresponding dilated and sheared version. We prove a Weyl-Minkowski inequality that holds for convex bodies under certain conditions, and the inequality takes its sharpest form in (n-1)-dimensional space. Notably, this inequality can be used to derive the anisotropic Sobolev trace inequality.

The Microscope space test of the weak equivalence principle (TEST) uses precise accelerometers to measure the acceleration experienced by two test masses in a microgravity environment. These accelerometers are designed to detect extremely small differences in acceleration, as small as 10^-15 g, which would indicate a violation of the TEST. However, sudden changes in acceleration, or glitches, can interfere with this measurement. A thorough examination of the data collected by the Microscope satellite reveals that these glitches are not random and exhibit a frequency that varies over time. As a result, the uncertainty in the test's outcome is influenced by the specific periods during which the satellite is in operation. A theoretical model has been developed to explain the origin of these glitches, taking into account the effects of the satellite's movement and the forces acting upon it. This model also allows for the calculation of the uncertainty in the test's result, which is found to be 10^-14 g for the data collected so far.

Self-assembling structures in soft matter systems can undergo dynamic changes in response to varying environmental conditions, which can be harnessed to create adaptive materials. A numerical model simulates the behavior of active colloidal molecules that interact through steric repulsion and short-range forces, and are subjected to an activity gradient. As a result of this gradient, the colloidal molecules become polarized, leading to the formation of dimer structures. When the activity levels are increased, a phase transition occurs, and dimer structures are replaced by more complex cyclic arrangements. These cyclic structures are stable as long as the activity gradient is moderate, but a decrease in activity leads to a return to the polarized dimer state. This research demonstrates that dynamic, reversible structures can be achieved with active colloidal molecules that self-assemble, which has implications for the development of responsive and reversible materials.

Strong shortest path collections are a refined version of shortest path collections, deeply linked to the concept of network node monitoring. The task of node monitoring using shortest paths can be likened to choosing a set of minimum strong shortest path collection sizes for a specific graph type. This paper addresses the minimum strong shortest path collection sizes for certain graph types, including grid, torus, Mobius strip, and toroidal triangular grids, and provides a set of grid-like graphs. Additionally, it presents an algorithm to identify the minimum strong shortest path collection sizes for a specific graph type.

The color dipole gluon PDF, which is non-zero only at the highest order in small-x, is found to be sensitive to both infrared and ultraviolet renormalons. The presence of an infrared renormalon at B=2 implies that the color dipole gluon PDF is inherently impacted by power-suppressed corrections of the form $O(\Lambda_{QCD}^2/Q^2)$ when measured in transverse momentum. As a consequence, the gluon TMD PDF becomes ambiguous due to the presence of such power corrections. The impact of this Sivers effect is further highlighted by the fact that the color dipole gluon PDF is the leading small-x contribution to the linearly suppressed term in the power expansion of the quark TMD PDF.

We analyze the frog model on a rooted tree with a degree of $d \geq 3$, where an active frog is initially placed at the root, and additional frogs are located at each edge of the tree, potentially multiple frogs per edge. Every active frog moves randomly along tree edges, and any encountered sleeping frog becomes active. We determine an exact exponent related to the density $\rho$ of frogs per edge, such that when $\rho$ exceeds this exponent, the frog model exhibits transient behavior, and when $\rho$ is less than this exponent, the model is recurrent. Our findings indicate that for a tree of degree $d$, the crucial density is exactly $d-1$.

Hybrid devices that integrate spintronic and photonic technologies have significant potential for high-speed, low-power information processing. To achieve this, researchers are developing photonic crystals with asymmetric characteristics using self-assembling methods. However, conventional methods, such as etching, cannot control the directionality of the resulting photonic crystals. We have successfully created a novel, direction-controlled photonic crystal by employing magnetically responsive particles in a process called magnetophotonic self-assembly. Our assembly process produces a surface lattice with distinct properties, enabling the differentiation of wavelengths and the direction of light. This research paves the way for creating low-cost, scalable, and efficient photonic crystals with controlled characteristics.

We've developed a novel method to transfer knowledge from an unseen, black-box model that's been trained on a vast amount of data, to a smaller model that's been trained on an unknown number of unlabeled images. The unknown model is assumed to have been trained using decision-based feedback, which is a common method for improving model performance.

Researchers have analyzed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay based on four distinct categories of events, yielding a branching fraction of $(8.4\pm0.6\pm0.3)\times10^{-4}$. Additionally, there is sufficient evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} ( \bar{D}^{*0}\to\bar{D}^0 \gamma)$ decay, with a significance of 3.5 standard deviations, and a corresponding branching fraction of $(5.4\pm1.0\pm0.4)\times10^{-4}$.

We present an efficient method to construct the lattice of submodules of a specific type of representation, specifically those that are sum of distinct irreducible modules, based on partial lattice information about the representations of its constituent irreducible components. This method enables us to effectively build the lattice of submodules of its composition series, which in turn provides valuable insights into constructing the lattice of self-shrinking submodules of $S_\lambda \mathbb{F}$, a challenging problem that has long resisted solution.

A geodetic set in a graph is defined as a set that forms the shortest possible distance from any other vertex in the graph. A geodetic recognition problem involves identifying whether a specific graph is geodetic or contains the minimum number of edge additions to make it geodetic. A graph is considered minimally geodetic if removing any edge results in a non-geodetic graph. This paper focuses on the computational complexity of determining if a given graph is minimally geodetic or recognizing geodetic and minimal geodetic subgraphs within another graph. We establish that the minimally geodetic recognition problem is coNP-complete, while the geodetic and minimal geodetic subset problems are NP-complete. Additionally, we provide polynomial-time solutions for bipartite and circular arc graphs, and a geometric characterization of minimally geodetic circular arc graphs.

When it comes to high-stakes real-world tasks, expert demonstrations are often used to teach machines the required skills.  However, getting a comprehensive set of perfect demonstrations can be costly and time-consuming.  As a result, researchers have developed imitation learning methods that learn from a mix of perfect demonstrations and random samples.  Unfortunately, many of these methods struggle with a large amount of suboptimal data.  They either fail to utilize the abundant distribution of experiences effectively or require assumptions that are hard to meet in practice.  To bridge this gap, we introduce TRAIL, a new algorithm that utilizes a range of data qualities, from optimal to suboptimal, and guarantees near-optimal performance with a large amount of suboptimal data.  TRAIL's efficiency can be improved with better demonstrations, and it outperforms the current state-of-the-art imitation learning algorithms in various simulated environments.

Reinforcement learning has been effectively improved through imitation learning, which utilizes expert knowledge to guide the training process. However, obtaining and utilizing expert knowledge is often a costly and impractical endeavor. Imitation learning can be made more efficient by utilizing data from multiple sources, which has been shown to yield better results. We investigate the imitating an unknown coach while being trained on an unspecified task, and we find that such training is prone to learning suboptimal policies. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called Co-Imitation Training, which involves learning and utilizing data from two sources. Implied by this approach, we propose a new algorithm that prevents the model from being misled by the flawed knowledge from the coach, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through both simulated and real-world experiments.

This research focuses on developing a method for calculating the performance and key metrics of error-correcting codes, specifically the maximum information transfer rate and error correction capability under various conditions. A case study is conducted with the [11, 5] quasi-cyclic code to demonstrate the calculation process and error correction ability, utilizing both a suboptimal algorithm and an optimal search method. Furthermore, a code is introduced to enhance the efficiency of the suboptimal algorithm.

Recent research has demonstrated that adding a reinforcement learning (RL) step after a translation model trained with supervised learning can enhance its performance. However, applying RL is challenging due to the large action space, which consists of all possible next tokens. In this study, we overcome this hurdle by utilizing a reinforcement learning stage with a small action space, which determines the probabilities of selecting the next token from an altered distribution. We train this small action space using a simple policy gradient method based on a performance metric. We integrate this RL refinement step after a translation model trained with supervised learning and observe significant performance gains on the ICLB14 and WMT14 English-to-French datasets. Notably, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art ensemble method on these datasets. We release our code to facilitate reproducibility.

A novel method for a robot to autonomously calibrate a depth camera and estimate the pose of its end-effector using only a set of marked targets has been developed. Initially, the robot learns to adjust the camera's settings to recognize the targets with a high degree of accuracy through a single trial. Subsequently, it employs machine learning to estimate the pose of its end-effector based on the images captured by the depth camera, given known target information. Experimental tests conducted with a real robot demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, which requires minimal training and can operate effectively with an uncalibrated camera.

This study focuses on the quark-flip-singling QFS and its associated QFS-region, a quasi-2D state characterized by a high degree of entanglement. Using a one-dimensional spin chain model, we explore the quark-flip-singling transition and its related properties, including a hysteresis phenomenon and persistent entanglement within the QFS-region. A theoretical model is proposed to describe the QFS-region, and we demonstrate that it can be experimentally observed through measurements of the overlap between initial and final states.

The rise of online news consumption has been accompanied by growing political polarization, particularly in the US. This research aims to analyze the political leanings of online news sources and examine how political polarization is reflected in the consumption patterns of online readers. By leveraging large-scale datasets from the SharedIt service, we were able to collect over 100 million sharing records and associated user profiles from 100 million unique sharing events. Through the application of topic modeling and user profiling techniques, we were able to categorize the political leanings of news articles and users, as well as identify the factors driving the political polarization observed in online news consumption. Our findings reveal a significant increase in political polarization over time, with the most pronounced rise occurring between 2016 and 2017. This increase in polarization is primarily driven by a rise in the consumption of partisan news, rather than mainstream news. Additionally, our research highlights the role of user demographics in shaping the political leanings of online news consumers, with older and more highly educated users tending to exhibit more polarized consumption patterns.

We investigate the word problem of the Thompson group V, which can be broken down using various subgroups, including a strong configuration property that allows us to analyze specific components. This property, when combined with known results, leads to the conclusion that some subgroup interactions have highly complex rewriting systems. These outcomes, when viewed through the lens of V's structure, reveal that even though V is a simple group, many of its finite index subgroups have unsolvable word problems. This has implications for understanding the relationship between V's simplicity and the computational complexity of its subgroups.

This paper presents both experimental and theoretical findings related to a two-level quantum system, specifically a superconducting qubit, that has been driven by microwave signals and is interacting with its surrounding environment. The system has reached a non-equilibrium steady state, which is independent of the initial state, as a result of periodic driving. We have experimentally observed this condition and compared it to the theoretical model of a qubit coupled to a 'bath' of two coupled harmonic oscillators, which is also being driven. The agreement between the non-equilibrium density matrix of the qubit and a effective Boltzmann distribution, derived from the bath's Hamiltonian and drive parameters, demonstrates that the driven bath has populated distinct energy levels. This finding has significant implications for understanding how to control and utilize driven systems in the context of quantum technologies.

We explore how certain advanced geometric concepts, specifically mean curvature operators and shape operators that follow periodic and semi-regular patterns of change, relate to the structure of higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. We then identify and analyze hypersurfaces that exhibit this behavior and possess a specific property where a subbundle of tangent spaces is orthogonal and invariant under the biharmonic mapping, ultimately demonstrating the unique structure of these biharmonic hypersurfaces.

Given positive integers $p$ and $q$ that share no common factors, a set $I$ consisting of non-negative integers less than $p$ is considered $p/q$-identifiable if for any two distinct sequences $a$ and $b$ made up of elements from $I$, the rational numbers represented by these sequences in base $p$ remain different when divided by $q$. This concept was initially explored by S. Berloche, S. Gravier, and L. Tougne in 2014. In this study, we focus on identifying the most comprehensive $p/q$-identifiable sets that are constructed using consecutive integers.

We propose a new form of matter known as "shadow matter," consisting of sterile neutrinos with a mass in the eV range that are coupled to axions with a muon decay width of approximately $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-6}$ eV. This coupling enables shadow matter to form compact objects like stars and black holes through non-gravitational interactions. As an alternative to dark matter, it could potentially be detectable via direct detection experiments. In this paper, we focus on axion-neutrino black holes and show that they can be created in mergers of neutron stars and black-hole-neutron star systems. These objects emit axion and sterile neutrino radiation, which can be detected as a distinct feature in gravitational wave signals. We also explore the implications of these findings on the abundance of such objects in the universe and their effects on the cosmic microwave background radiation. Our results suggest that only sterile neutrinos with a mass between 2.6 eV and 4.5 eV can account for all the shadow matter in the universe. This range of masses is consistent with the observed stability of the Milky Way galaxy. We also show that the required parameters for these black holes can be detected by future direct detection experiments like ADMX and ADMX+.

The LAMOST Time-Domain Survey (LTS) is set to significantly enhance our understanding of transient phenomena and stellar variability by conducting a comprehensive study of 100,000 variable stars and 10,000 transient sources, with a high cadence of observations at least four times per night. The LAMOST 7-m telescope, with its 8 spectroscopic stations, has the capability to observe four $K$2 plates each night, with the potential to increase the survey's cadence to nightly observations. The spectroscopic data collected by LAMOST offers unique insights into stellar variability and transient sources that photometric surveys cannot provide. The current study focuses on the initial results of the LAMOST 58hm variable star database, with a high fraction of stars exhibiting significant variability, with at least 40% classified as such. The variability periods of these stars span a wide range, from less than one hour to over 100 days, with the most common periods falling between one and ten hours. The variable stars studied exhibit diverse spectral types, with the most common being K, M, and S types. The study also highlights the unique advantages of using spectroscopic data to investigate stellar variability and transient sources, with the LAMOST 7-m telescope being an ideal instrument for this purpose.

A cutting-plane operation called graph-cut is frequently used for 2D and 3D medical image segmentation, but it has limitations due to its inability to account for spatial continuity and its reliance on boundary information. To address these issues, we propose a novel approach that combines graph-cut with a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) in an edge-gated manner. This method allows the DCNN to focus on relevant boundary information while maintaining the inherent strengths of graph-cut in terms of smoothness and closure. Experiments conducted on public datasets (Berkeley Segmentation Dataset and Spleen dataset) demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, yielding improved results compared to state-of-the-art methods.

MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database that provides various modes of data access, including features for creating persistent data and ensuring transactional consistency through indexed documents and documents collections. However, no verified transactional coherence systems have been established for the MongoDB. To address this issue, we have developed a translation tool that converts a transactional coherence specification for indexed documents into a corresponding coherence protocol, which we named tMongo. We have also created an implementation of tMongo for the MongoDB and conducted a transactional coherence validation using a co-simulation approach. Furthermore, we have compared the performance of tMongo with the native behavior of indexed documents and found that it offers improved latency and throughput in certain scenarios.

Hosono and Kim demonstrated the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric functions for specific trees, utilizing a combinatorial interpretation of the inverse Kostka array. This paper extends that work by providing an $e$-positivity proof for the chromatic symmetric functions of certain trees through a new combinatorial interpretation of the inverse Kostka array. This expanded interpretation encompasses the previous ones offered by Kim-Hosono and Pan.

This paper introduces a contrastive learning framework for functional areas of the brain, specifically the executive function. We model the working memory as a process that learns to resample and relabel sensory input through a contrastive value strategy known as "hindsight summarization." We demonstrate that this approach can lead to the emergence of working memory characteristics and executive function capabilities. Building on this model, we incorporate an area to generate new ideas, or "planning," to create a more advanced version of the network. This allows for task performance testing and visualization of executive function and working memory characteristics. We also explore the role of prefrontal cortex lesions in this context.

Deep neural networks excel at solving complex pattern recognition tasks, including extracting relevant features from medical images. However, these images often contain inherent biases that can mislead the DNNs and lead to biased performance. Although researchers have developed methods to assess bias in images for certain applications, a comprehensive understanding of innate bias in medical images is still lacking. In this study, we explore innate bias identification in medical images, a crucial step towards addressing bias in these images. To address this challenge, we propose a method to evaluate bias in medical images and a dataset to train and test models. Our proposed bias identification model uses a simple yet effective approach to assess innate bias in medical images. Our experiments show that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art models in identifying bias in medical images. In this study, we provide a detailed analysis of innate bias identification in medical images, a crucial step towards addressing bias in these images.

This study delves into the hidden structural and dynamic complexities of intricate systems using a specialized model of nanoscale assemblies that exhibit different types of interactions. By applying concepts of graph theory, we uncover how magnetic properties and assembly patterns are influenced by the way components interact, specifically through triangular relationships and pairwise interactions. We find that certain types of triangular interactions can lead to unique magnetic states and stability, while an increase in certain pairwise interactions can lead to a sudden shift in magnetic properties and stability. This research highlights the critical role that concealed geometry plays in determining the behavior of complex systems and has broader implications for understanding and manipulating magnetic properties in other types of intricate assemblies.

A phenomenon known as solar breeze occurs in the inner heliosphere, where the Sun continuously emits charged particles into space. As the Parker Solar Probe approaches the Sun, it will collect breeze data and compare it to solar wind observations made by other spacecraft. The probe's unique capabilities allow it to measure the mass flux of charged particles flowing out from the Sun with unprecedented precision. Measurements taken so far show a power-law relationship between mass flux and distance from the Sun, following an exponent of -2, which is consistent with theoretical models of a ballistic outflow. The probe's advanced instruments will enable it to make detailed observations of the inner heliosphere, providing valuable insights into the formation of heliospheric transients and the forces that shape the Sun's influence on the solar system.

Speech-emotion recognition is a crucial task in the speech-emotion identification process. This paper proposes a novel approach, called domain-adapted deep reinforcement learning, to improve speech-emotion recognition performance. We employ a deep reinforcement learning model, specifically a Q-learning algorithm, to fine-tune the speech-emotion recognition model. The model's output is used to provide feedback to the reinforcement learning algorithm, which in turn adjusts the model's parameters to optimize its performance. We also incorporate domain adaptation techniques to account for differences between training and testing data. Our experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches, particularly in terms of accuracy and robustness.

We investigated the structural and magnetic properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under increasing pressure up to 10 GPa using X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and the nuclear forward scattering technique. Our findings revealed that Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ undergoes a phase transition at approximately 7.5 GPa, which is accompanied by a change in the magnetic behavior of the Fe$^{3+}$ ions. The initial magnetic phase is characterized by long-range ordering, which is verified by the observation of a magnetic hyperfine field. The application of pressure causes the magnetic phase to shift to a low-spin state, which is indicated by a decrease in the magnetic hyperfine field. The structural changes observed in Bi$_5$FeTi$_{3}$O$_{15}$ under elevated pressure are also consistent with the changes in its magnetic properties. The study provides valuable insights into the relationship between the crystal structure and magnetism in Aurivillius phase materials under pressure.

This research paper introduces a method to estimate the accuracy of numerical solutions in discrete-continuous shortest path optimization problems. The problems considered involve finding optimal routes with associated costs, and the solutions are obtained using a technique called homotopy continuation. The methodology is demonstrated in the context of flight path optimization, specifically in determining the most cost-effective trajectory that adheres to a given destination and starting time constraints. A specific numerical approach, involving direct collocation and a line search, is employed to derive a cost estimate for the optimal trajectory. The accuracy of the solutions is assessed through a set of test problems and real-world flight data, and the resulting cost bounds are applied to optimize a flight from New York to Paris.

Researchers have extensively studied the effects of intense shock waves on the universe, particularly those caused by supernovae explosions. In this study, we investigate the behavior of a shock wave in an expanding universe with a spherical void, focusing on the interaction between the two. By using a uniform expansion model and the BSSN formalism, we examine the behavior of the shock wave and the fluid behind it. Our results show that the interaction between the void and the shock wave causes a complex pattern of expansion and contraction, with the void's size increasing and decreasing over time. In addition, our results show that the interaction between the void and the shock wave causes a change in the density and velocity of the fluid behind it, with the density decreasing and the velocity increasing over time. In order to better understand the behavior of the universe with intense shock waves, further research is needed to explore the effects of these waves on the formation of galaxies and the distribution of matter in the universe.

Researchers have determined the differential decay rate for the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ process, utilizing a sample of 3.49 inverse femtobarns of data from the LHCb experiment. By reconstructing the $D_s^{*-}$ through its decay products, specifically the $D_s^{-}$ and the associated photon, they have obtained a precise measurement of the differential decay rate, which is expressed as $d\Gamma/ds_{\mu\nu}(\bar{D_s^-}\gamma) = (0.101 \pm 0.014 \pm 0.006) \times 10^{-4}$ picobarns.

A new class of orthogonal functions is identified as generalized Hermite polynomials, which include classical Hermite polynomials and Laguerre-Hermite polynomials. It is demonstrated that these functions serve as exact eigenstates for Schrödinger operators with potentials that do not have unique monodromy. Furthermore, it is found that generalized Lamé potentials, which are defined by third-order differential equations, can be made to correspond to unique monodromy when combined with non-Abelian gauge fields. This connection is established through the use of Darboux transformations.

The unpredictable behavior of self-organized criticality (SOC) models has long been theorized to occur in nature, yet experimental evidence has been scarce due to the difficulty of measuring small-scale fluctuations. A recent study provides a straightforward method to measure crackling noise, capturing the dynamic process of peeling adhesive tape, which exhibits sudden releases of force as it separates into a series of fragments. By recording the sizes of these fragments, researchers discovered a critical exponent that differs from previous static measurements of SOC systems. This discovery highlights the complexity of measuring the dynamics of SOC and suggests that additional research is necessary to fully understand the phenomenon. The experiment's simplicity and direct observability make it an ideal model system for further investigation into the dynamics of SOC.

Our research focuses on planar Josephson junctions and small SQUIDs fabricated from molybdenum silicide, specifically designed to investigate the effects of magnetic fields on superconducting devices. By applying two perpendicular magnetic fields, we can manipulate a phase variable within the order parameter, allowing us to measure the critical current as a function of this phase. The critical current in our devices exhibits a characteristic 4π-periodic behavior, in contrast to the typical 2π periodicity observed in conventional devices. The results indicate that a population of devices with half-integer fluxoid values exhibits enhanced critical currents, in comparison to devices with integer values. The observed behavior is consistent with predictions made by the BCS theory, in relation to the pair density of the devices under study.

The addition of a specific term to the Standard Model, known as the "abc term" or "non-abelian ether-like term," has significant implications for non-perturbative phenomena like sphaleron transitions. This term can be effectively described using a dimension-six operator, specifically (Tr($F_{\mu\nu}$)$\tilde{F}^{\mu\nu}$)/$\Lambda^2$. In this study, we examine the impact of this term on the Standard Model at finite temperature through both lattice simulations and thermal field theory. Our lattice simulations, which include dynamic quarks, are used to calculate the thermal phase transition and the electroweak sphaleron rate as a function of temperature. The results from our simulations are compared to analytical calculations, which show that the thermal sphaleron rate is influenced by the ether-like term in a way that is consistent with its zero-temperature behavior. Furthermore, we calculate the impact of this term on the Standard Model's effective potential at finite temperature, which is relevant for understanding the Standard Model's vacuum stability and the characteristics of the early universe.

When an option is sold, the seller must set aside a certain amount as a margin to cover potential losses from hedging. This paper derives a precise formula for the value of that margin under specific conditions: the underlying asset's price changes follow the Cox-Ross-Rubinstein model, and the cost of hedging is based on trading volume. The formula's accuracy is verified through numerical examples, and it can be used to determine the optimal margin requirements. The proposed equation is shown to be efficient in estimating the margin requirements, with results comparable to those obtained from more traditional methods like Monte Carlo simulations.

Within this domain, we have a high-contrast composite material characterized by a symmetric matrix $A$, which is defined as the ratio of two functions $a_1$ and $a_2$, both belonging to the class $L^\infty(\Omega)$. We utilized deep imaging data from the Subaru Prime-Survey to study tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies, determining their flux fraction. Our analysis revealed that approximately 10% of early-type galaxies exhibit tidal features with a flux fraction exceeding 10%. By comparing our findings with a previous Hubble survey of nearby galaxies, we observed a similar tidal feature fraction across different distance ranges, suggesting that tidal mergers occur at a rate that is independent of a galaxy's distance. Through theoretical modeling, we estimated a tidal merger rate of around $0.025 h$ per Gyr for $L^*$ galaxies, which is roughly twice the rate of major mergers required to form early-type galaxies from spiral galaxies. Our study suggests that tidal mergers between early-type galaxies play a significant role in galaxy evolution. Additionally, we discovered that the tidal tail morphology of early-type galaxies is often complex, with many galaxies exhibiting multiple tidal components. We also found that the tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies are more prominent in the local universe compared to high-redshift galaxies, which may be attributed to the difference in merger history between these two populations.

This research paper explores how to balance opportunities across generations in a dynamic model of social mobility, where individuals' positions are influenced by both economic fluctuations and intergenerational transfers of opportunities. The study's aim is to find a strategy for allocating these transfers that maximizes the balance of opportunities across generations, ultimately leading to a simplified approach for achieving this balance when conditions are more complex.

This paper presents key technologies and system designs for high-power lasers,
including green-seeded lasers, frequency conversion methods, and novel laser
design concepts like reverse engineering. It discusses the importance of
developing high-power, high-quality factor lasers for various applications,
including high-energy and high-precision systems. The paper outlines the
design process for high-power lasers, covering seed laser selection, system
architecture, and critical components. It also provides an overview of
high-power laser systems, including regenerative amplifiers, multi-pass systems,
and their respective operating principles and performance capabilities. The paper
further explores the concept of reverse engineering, which involves modifying
existing high-power laser systems to enhance their performance, and presents a
case study on upgrading a 100J-level Ti:Sapphire laser system. The paper's
conclusions highlight the significance of high-power laser systems in various
fields and the potential for further development through innovative technologies.

We prove that for any incompressible subset K of Lp (where 1 < p < 2), there is a sufficiently small positive number ε such that K can be isometrically embedded into a space with a dimension one lower than that required for J-near-isometric embeddings (where n is the dimension of the ambient space).

A new technique called brightness scans has been introduced to streamline beam diagnostics, specifically for drawing closed paths around a beam's cross-section. Unlike traditional methods, brightness scans can be executed using only diagonal measurements, streamlining the process. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and real beam measurements, revealing its capability to accurately capture beam properties, including overall dimensions and internal structure. The results show a high level of accuracy, with a maximum difference of 0.6mm when comparing brightness scans to the actual beam profile. Furthermore, the consistency of the measured beam current is within 1% across different brightness scans. The reduced measurement time afforded by this technique enables more frequent diagnostics, facilitating improved beam control.

This paper introduces a distributed optimization algorithm that enables agents to share information and communicate with each other in order to solve the problem. The proposed method is robust against malicious attacks, ensuring that the system can handle unreliable data from malicious agents. A proof of convergence is provided for the algorithm, and a numerical example is used to demonstrate its effectiveness. The results show that the algorithm converges to an optimal solution at a rate of $O(1/k)$, where $k$ is the iteration number. The study also reveals that the convergence rate is influenced by the number of agents and the strength of the malicious attack. The results provide a foundation for the development of more advanced distributed optimization algorithms that can be used in a variety of applications, including multi-agent systems and the Internet of Things. Precision measurements of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) require accurate modeling of instrumental biases to effectively separate the primary cosmological signals from noise and foregrounds. To advance this research, reliable simulations of real CMB experiments are crucial. This paper presents an update to the Simulations for the 4th Generation CMB Experiments package (s4cmb), which now incorporates the latest survey designs and data processing methods from experiments like BICEP/Keck, S4, and Simons Observatory. The updates to s4cmb include new simulations of the 2018 BICEP2/Keck Array combined data, which are used to validate a new method for estimating the 217 GHz spectral amplitude parameter $r$ that yields results consistent with the published findings. The s4cmb package is also employed to generate realistic simulations of the 2021 BICEP/Keck combined data, which yield a more precise estimate of $r$ and a more accurate estimate of the level of submillimeter foregrounds. The s4cmb package is further utilized to generate realistic simulations of the Simons Observatory and Simultaneous Simons Array Cross-correlation experiments, which are expected to produce highly precise estimates of $r$ and the levels of submillimeter foregrounds in the future.

In the current research landscape, leveraging pre-trained language models for enhancing or substituting morphology and word order learning in Word Arrangement (WA) is relatively uncommon. To investigate the role of pre-trained language models in word arrangement learning, we conducted an experiment using BART, a state-of-the-art pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model. We found that using BART for morphology and word order learning is highly effective, resulting in a significant improvement of 10.45% in mean absolute error compared to the best existing baseline. Furthermore, BART's training can be optimized by incorporating additional training data, reducing the amount of morphology and word order data required. We also explored the possibility of using BART for low-resource languages, and found that it can effectively transfer knowledge from high-resource languages to low-resource languages.

Deepfakes are a type of deceptive media created using advanced production techniques and AI-driven methods that mimic real individuals. This deceptive content poses significant risks, ranging from personal embarrassment to severe consequences such as political instability and financial loss. Deepfake detection is a critical task that requires identifying and distinguishing between real and deceptive media. One widely used deepfake generation technique is the generative adversarial network (GAN). GAN-based methods consist of two key components: an encoder that extracts meaningful information from real images and a decoder that generates deceptive images. Existing deepfake detection approaches often focus on specific parts of these methods, such as swapping the real image's features with those of the fake image. This technique, however, is computationally expensive and does not consider other factors such as inconsistencies in eye movements and facial expressions. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called the multi-domain cross-stitched network (MD-CSDNetwork). This framework, which is based on the idea of cross-network stitching, allows us to extract complementary information from two networks and integrate it with the image's original features. By doing so, our approach is able to capture a more comprehensive set of features that characterize deepfake images. Experimental results on two widely used deepfake datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Current research on the binary deletion channel primarily focuses on linear-channel coding techniques. In contrast, this study investigates the effectiveness of non-linear low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with degree-degree correlations for modeling the binary deletion channel. By adapting an existing LDPC code construction, we modify the code's degree-degree check matrix to better suit the binary deletion channel. This modification involves assigning adjacent bits to check nodes based on their Hamming distance. As a result, our modified LDPC codes exhibit improved error-correction capabilities compared to conventional LDPC codes with random degree-degree check matrices of the same length and density. However, these modified codes may suffer from a higher error floor due to the presence of short cycles in their Tanner graphs. A proposed technique to mitigate this issue is to adjust the code's degree distribution to minimize the occurrence of two-cycles.

A novel, secure method for implementing the decoy-state protocol was previously proposed, which involves randomizing the phase of the signal and decoy states within a specific range of $-\pi$ to $0$. This method aims to prevent an attacker from obtaining information about the phase and intensity of the transmitted states. However, it was discovered that an attacker could still execute a sophisticated attack called the coherent superposition attack, which bypasses the security measures and results in an increased key allocation rate. A new attack vector was identified, which involves manipulating the interference between the phase of the transmitted states and a malicious device controlled by the attacker. This attack exploits a vulnerability in the system and leads to an unintended increase in the allocated key rate. A theoretical framework was developed to analyze the impact of this attack on the system's performance and to provide a solution to mitigate its effects.

To maintain optimal performance of 5G mobile networks, periodic core network reconfiguration is necessary. This reconfiguration can be facilitated by a core network reoptimizer, which leverages historical network data to identify and adjust suboptimal configurations. A core network configuration consists of multiple interconnected components, including routing, link management, and control plane settings. In this research, a core network reoptimizer framework is proposed, which employs a reinforcement learning-based reconfiguration algorithm to refine core network settings. The proposed framework is then evaluated through a series of simulations, which demonstrate its ability to effectively optimize core network configurations and improve overall network performance. Furthermore, a core network reconfiguration management system is proposed, which integrates the proposed reinforcement learning-based reconfiguration algorithm with a core network reconfiguration database, which stores core network configuration data and enables periodic reconfiguration and real-time configuration adjustment. This system is designed to be user-friendly and intuitive, which enables network administrators to easily monitor and manage core network configurations through a web-based interface.

In 1923, Menger laid the groundwork for metric geometry by defining a new type of space, the angle metric space, through a specific relation between metrics. Menger had envisioned an axiomatic approach to develop the properties of such spaces. The author of this paper demonstrates that the axioms proposed by Menger for the existence of a angle metric space are satisfied by the Euclidean metric if and only if a particular set of conditions is met. The author also proves that the conditions for the satisfaction of Menger's axioms are equivalent to the conditions for the satisfaction of Menger's third axiom, thereby showing that the angle metric relation is equivalent to the standard Euclidean metric. The author also provides a similar condition for the satisfaction of Menger's fourth axiom. The article's findings are crucial in resolving the longstanding issues raised by Menger regarding the nature of angle metrics in the context of Euclidean metrics. The author's research is an essential contribution to the field of metric geometry and has significant implications for the development of the field.
